Why does this query ignore the index on email?

SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.c'

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=build|construct=ai_engineer|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The index is ordered by the raw email. LOWER(email) is a different value, so the planner cannot walk that order. It will scan unless there is an index on the expression LOWER(email), or the predicate is rewritten to a range on the raw column, which LOWER does not allow. Comparing email = 'a@b.c' would use the index and would miss rows stored in other cases. The fix that keeps case-insensitivity is an expression index, plus storing a normalized column if they will query it constantly.
</think>

LOWER(email) hides the column from an index on email. Index the expression, or store a normalized email and compare that.
We retry failed card charges from a worker. A 201 that was actually saved, followed by a timeout on the response, gets charged again. Fix the shape, not the vendor.

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=build|construct=ai_engineer|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
The worker treats a missing response as a failed charge. The charge already happened. The fix is an idempotency key stored before the call, unique on the order id, and the retry sends the same key. The vendor then returns the original 201 instead of a second charge. A local 'did we already try' flag that is written after the response never runs in the timeout case, which is why it doesn't work. Write the key first.
</think>

Put an idempotency key on the order before the call, and send that same key on the retry. A flag written after the response never gets set when the response is what timed out.
p95 latency went from 40ms to 400ms after we raised the pool from 10 connections to 100. The database CPU is idle. What do you look at first?

<think>
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=build|construct=ai_engineer|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
Idle CPU means the database is not doing more work. It is waiting, or the app is. A pool of 100 against a database that is happy often means lock wait, or the app is now scheduling so many requests that they pile up on a saturated client. First graph is lock waits and the app's runnable queue, not a bigger pool. Raising the pool again would add waiters. Also check that the new pool didn't disable prepared statements or move to a transaction mode that holds locks longer. The idle CPU is the clue that capacity is not the missing piece.
</think>

Look at lock waits and the app's own queue, not the database CPU. The pool grew and the database is idle, so the time is waiting, not computing. Don't raise the pool further until you see the wait.
